- From \( d_i = 0 \), the possible next digits are \( 2 \).
- From \( d_i = 1 \), the possible next digits are \( 3 \).
- From \( d_i = 2 \), the possible next digits are \( 0 \) or \( 4 \).
- From \( d_i = 3 \), the possible next digits are \( 1 \) or \( 5 \).

- From \( d_i = 5 \), the possible next digits are \( 3 \) or \( 7 \) (but since 7 is not in the set, it is not possible).
- From \( d_i = 6 \), the possible next digits are \( 4 \).

We can represent the transition probabilities as a Markov chain with the following transition matrix:
\[
P = \begin{pmatrix}
0 & \frac{1}{6} & \frac{1}{6} & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
\frac{1}{6} & 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{6} & \frac{1}{6} & 0 & 0 \\
0 & \frac{1}{6} & 0 & 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{6} & \frac{1}{6} \\
0 & 0 & \frac{1}{6} & 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{6} & \frac{1}{6} \\
\frac{1}{6} & 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{6} & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & \frac{1}{6} & \frac{1}{6} & 0 & \frac{1}{6} & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{6}
\end{pmatrix}
\]

The number of 12-digit words can be computed as the initial state vector raised to the 12th power:
\[
\mathbf{v}^{(12)} = P^{12} \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}

Since each move corresponds to a change of 2 units, and the first and last digits are 0 and 6, the number of "up" moves must be exactly 6 (since \( 6 - 0 = 6 \), and each up move adds 2 units).
